title: The model's safest patients
hook: In toy records, asthma patients with pneumonia die less. What if a model acts on that?

knows: a model learns patterns from past records
doesNotKnow: that records carry the effects of past decisions, so a model that predicts well can give the wrong answer to 'what should we do?', and acting on it removes the very care that made the pattern

misconception: If a model trained on hospital records predicts accurately that a group dies less, that group is low risk and can safely get less care.
objective: The learner can explain that asthma patients died less in the records because they all got intensive care, so a model that ranks them lowest risk and sends them to the ward raises their deaths: prediction from past records is not the effect of changing care.

claims.text: Under the old rule (every asthma patient to intensive care), 2 of 50 asthma patients (4%) and 12 of 150 others (8%) die; the toy risks are stated on the stage: ward 20% for asthma and 8% for others, intensive care cuts asthma's to 4%.
claims.source: 50 x 0.04 = 2, 150 x 0.08 = 12 (exact expected counts, no sampling); outcome('old') in Demo.tsx. Brief 57, company/domains/briefs/ai.ai-society.md. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Own node: ASTHMA_DIE_ICU has 2 of 50 (pc 4%), OTHERS_DIE (o mod 25 in {3,16}) has 12 of 150 (8%), total 14. Stage message before 'Model's view': 'Ward risk: asthma 20%, others 8%. Intensive care: asthma 4%.' (0.2*100, 0.08*100, 0.04*100 print as 20, 8, 4 exactly). Counts are exact expected deaths: 0.04*50 = 2, 0.08*150 = 12.

claims.text: A model fitted to those records ranks asthma as the lowest-risk group (stage: "Model's view of the old records: asthma 4% risk, others 8%. Safest: asthma.").
claims.source: The toy model is the group death rate in the old records: 2/50 = 4% < 12/150 = 8%. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): DISPUTED. Substance unchanged. Needs a fresh fact-check. | FC pass 36 (fact-checker, fresh instance, 2026-10-14, W-637): VERIFIED (v2). Safest: asthma.`; own node renders it as "Model's view of the old records: asthma 4% risk, others 8%. Safest: asthma." and the claim text contains that string exactly (ASCII apostrophe). 2/50 = 4% < 12/150 = 8% (OTHERS_DIE: o mod 25 in {3,16}, 12 dots), so the group-rate model ranks asthma lowest; reveal says 'ranked asthma as the safest group'.

claims.text: When the model's ranking sends asthma patients to the ward, 10 of 50 (20%) die; the others stay at 12 of 150.
claims.source: 50 x 0.20 = 10; outcome('model') in Demo.tsx (ASTHMA_DIE_WARD has 10 entries, OTHERS_DIE 12). Total deaths rise from 14 to 22 (not in learner text). | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Own node: under 'Model decides care' the asthma deaths are ASTHMA_DIE_WARD, 10 of 50 = 20% (0.2*50 = 10); OTHERS_DIE is the same set under both rules, 12 of 150. Reveal prints MODEL.asthma = 10 of 50. The 2 ICU deaths (dots 7, 32) are inside the 10, so no dot switches from dead to alive.

claims.text: The patients, their risks and which dots die are a toy, labelled on the stage ('Toy pneumonia patients'); the dying dots are a fixed list, not a chosen seed.
claims.source: Brief 57. The real-world pattern this toy echoes: Caruana, Lou, Gehrke, Koch, Sturm and Elhadad (2015), 'Intelligible models for healthcare: predicting pneumonia risk and hospital 30-day readmission', KDD 2015 (a model learned that asthma lowers pneumonia death risk because asthmatic patients had been admitted directly to intensive care); Cooper et al. (1997), Artificial Intelligence in Medicine 9(2). The citation is not in learner text; if a later version names it, it needs the fact-checker. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Convention: tag 'Toy pneumonia patients' is always on the stage; deaths come from constant arrays (ASTHMA_DIE_WARD, ASTHMA_DIE_ICU, OTHERS_DIE by modulus), with no RNG or seed anywhere in Demo.tsx.

claims.text: A model that predicts well from past records answers 'who did badly before?', not 'what happens if we change what we do?'.
claims.source: The toy: the model's prediction (asthma 4%) was accurate for the old records, yet acting on it changed asthma's death rate to 20%, because the records were produced by a care policy the action removed. Standard prediction-versus-intervention distinction (Pearl, Causality, 2nd ed. 2009, ch. 1, do-operator); Caruana et al. (2015) above. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Derivation inside the toy: the old-records ranking (asthma 4%, others 8%) is an accurate description of past outcomes, yet acting on it moves asthma deaths from 2 to 10 because the records carried the effect of ICU care. That is the distinction the sentence states. Interpretive, consistent with the stage; no external fact.

recall.question: In a firm's records, staff who got a mentor rarely quit, because managers gave mentors to people at risk of leaving. A model trained on the records says those people are safe. What happens if HR stops their mentoring on that advice?
options: More of them quit: the records showed the mentoring working, not low risk
Nothing: the model predicted accurately, so they are low risk
Fewer quit, because the model found the safe group
recall.why: The records carry the effect of a past decision. A model can predict who quit before without knowing what happens when you change what you do.
